note: Generated by sync/build_catalog.py. Catalogue positions are the source of truth: right ascension in hours, declination in degrees, distance in light-years. Cartesian coordinates are derived at load time by CelestialCoordinates.EquatorialToUniverseFromLightYears, in astronomical units, with Earth at the origin. Nothing here is pre-projected or compressed. radiusAstronomicalUnits is the real physical radius of primaryBody; markerAngularSizeDegrees is only a floor on how small the object may look on screen. firstSeen is the day this pipeline first saw the object and never changes afterwards. Solar system bodies are a snapshot: their positions are computed for the generated date above, because unlike everything else here, they move. Spacecraft in Earth orbit are the exception to the whole scheme: they carry tleLine1 and tleLine2 instead of a position, and their right ascension and declination are unused placeholders set to zero. A position computed here would be on the far side of the planet within the hour, so the app propagates the orbital elements against its own clock. See sync/sources/satellites.py.

The closest black hole known, found in 2022 by watching a Sun-like star orbit something invisible. It is dormant: nothing is falling in, so it gives off no light at all. Mass: 9.62 times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (GALEX J172841.0-003451); distance from parallax 2.07 mas, from SIMBAD. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary.

objects.fact: The first object ever widely accepted as a black hole. It pulls gas off a blue supergiant companion, and the gas glows in X-rays on the way down. Mass: 21.2 times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (HD 226868); distance from parallax 0.4439 mas, from SIMBAD. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary.

objects.fact: A black hole that goes quiet for decades and then erupts. Its 2015 outburst made it briefly one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky. Mass: 9 times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (V* V404 Cyg); distance from 2.39 kpc, from VLBI parallax (Miller-Jones et al. 2009), which is more precise here than the Gaia value. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary.

objects.fact: A microquasar that fires jets of gas outward at nearly the speed of light. It spins so fast that its event horizon turns close to the theoretical maximum. Mass: 12.4 times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (Granat 1915+105); distance from 8.6 kpc, from VLBI parallax (Reid et al. 2014). Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary. Jet direction from the superluminal ejections tracked at radio wavelengths (Mirabel and Rodriguez 1994); the two angles are approximate and published values differ.

objects.fact: The nearest active galaxy, split by a dark lane of dust. Radio jets reach a million light-years out from the black hole at its centre. Mass: 55 million times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (NAME Centaurus A); distance from 3.8 Mpc, from the tip of the red giant branch; the galaxy's own motion makes its redshift useless as a distance here. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary. Jet direction from the inner radio jet; published inclinations range from 50 to 80 degrees; the two angles are approximate and published values differ.

objects.fact: A black hole hidden behind a thick doughnut of gas and dust, seen edge-on. Neutrinos have been detected coming from it, which almost nothing else can claim. Mass: 17 million times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (M 77); distance from 14.4 Mpc, from maser and Tully-Fisher measurements. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary.

objects.fact: The first black hole ever photographed, at the heart of the giant galaxy M87. The ring of light the Event Horizon Telescope captured in 2019 is this object. Mass: 6.5 billion times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (M 87); distance from 16.4 Mpc, from surface brightness fluctuations (EHT Collaboration 2019). Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary. Jet direction from VLBI imaging of the jet; the small inclination is why the counter-jet is so much fainter; the two angles are approximate and published values differ.

objects.fact: Among the most massive black holes ever weighed. Its event horizon alone is wider than our entire solar system, and it sits at the centre of the Coma Cluster. Mass: 21 billion times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (NGC 4889); distance from light travel time for redshift z = 0.0215, flat LCDM with H0 = 67.4 and Om = 0.315. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary.

objects.fact: A jet pointed almost straight at Earth. That geometry is why a galaxy this far away can flare brightly enough to be watched from night to night. Mass: 200 million times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (Z 184-50); distance from light travel time for redshift z = 0.03, flat LCDM with H0 = 67.4 and Om = 0.315. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary.

objects.fact: The brightest radio galaxy in the sky. Two jets end in enormous lobes of glowing gas, far outside the galaxy that launched them. Mass: 2.5 billion times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (MCG+07-41-003); distance from light travel time for redshift z = 0.05655, flat LCDM with H0 = 67.4 and Om = 0.315. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary. Jet direction from the axis between the two radio lobes, seen nearly side-on; the two angles are approximate and published values differ.

objects.fact: The first quasar ever recognised as one, in 1963, when its spectrum turned out to be enormously redshifted. It is the brightest quasar in our sky. Mass: 890 million times the Sun.
objects.source: Position from SIMBAD (3C 273); distance from light travel time for redshift z = 0.1576, flat LCDM with H0 = 67.4 and Om = 0.315. Radius is the Schwarzschild radius; mass is a published estimate and estimates vary. Jet direction from the optical and radio jet reaching south-west from the quasar, at a small angle to our line of sight; the two angles are approximate and published values differ.
